quote: There's lots of ways to be, as a person. And some people express their deep appreciation in different ways. But one of the ways that I believe people express their appreciation to the rest of humanity is to make something wonderful and put it out there.
notes: From Jobs's remarks at an internal Apple meeting on October 23, 2007. Verified via the Steve Jobs Archive (stevejobsarchive.com/stories/on-the-origin-of-make-something-wonderful).

quote: If ever there's a tomorrow when we're not together, there's something you must remember. [...] You're braver than you believe, and stronger than you seem, and smarter than you think. [...] But the most important thing is, even if we're apart, I'll always be with you.
attribution: Christopher Robin, Pooh's Grand Adventure: The Search for Christopher Robin (1997)
notes: Written by Carter Crocker and Karl Geurs for the Disney film. Popularly misattributed to A. A. Milne (dead 41 years before the line existed) and usually shortened to "You're braver than you believe..." with the roles flipped so Pooh says it to Christopher Robin. The film has "and stronger than you seem, and smarter than you think"; the poster version drops both "ands."

The sentence closes the opening paragraph of Ulrich's article "Vertuous Women Found: New England Ministerial Literature, 1668–1735" (American Quarterly, Spring 1976): an observation that pious women rarely entered the historical record, not a call to misbehave. It spread online from 1996 and was later credited to Marilyn Monroe and Eleanor Roosevelt.

quote: I can accept failure. Everyone fails at something. But I can't accept not trying.
notes: The title line of I Can't Accept Not Trying: Michael Jordan on the Pursuit of Excellence (HarperSanFrancisco, 1994), a 36-page book with photographs by Sandro Miller; library records credit the text to Jordan and the editing to Mark Vancil. Genuinely his, but usually shared without its source.

quote: He walked down, for a long while avoiding looking at her as at the sun, but seeing her, as one does the sun, without looking.
attribution: Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina (Part 1, Chapter 9), translated by Constance Garnett
notes: Levin watching Kitty skate at the Zoological Gardens, before he has proposed; not Vronsky and Anna. The common poster wording ("He stepped down, trying not to look long at her...") is not Garnett's and circulates with no translator named.

attribution: Darth Vader, The Empire Strikes Back (1980)
notes: The actual line. Popularly misremembered as "Luke, I am your father"; a 2022 YouGov poll found 62% of Americans recalled the wrong version and 17% the right one. On set David Prowse spoke placeholder dialogue and James Earl Jones recorded the real line later.

quote: I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.
notes: Written by Hall (pen name S. G. Tallentyre) in The Friends of Voltaire (1906) to sum up Voltaire's attitude when Helvétius's De l'esprit was burned, not to quote him. In 1935 she called it a paraphrase, and in a 1939 letter said it was "my own expression" that "should not have been put in inverted commas." Not found in Voltaire's works.

quote: The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results.
notes: Not found in Einstein's works; listed as misattributed in The Ultimate Quotable Einstein. Quote Investigator's earliest match is an Al-Anon item in the Knoxville News-Sentinel (October 11, 1981), then a November 1981 Narcotics Anonymous draft and Rita Mae Brown's Sudden Death (1983). The Einstein credit first appears in 1990.

quote: This we know. The earth does not belong to man; man belongs to the earth… Whatever befalls the earth befalls the sons of the earth. Man did not weave the web of life; he is merely a strand in it.
attribution: Attributed to Chief Seattle (actually written by Ted Perry)
notes: Written by Texas scriptwriter Ted Perry in 1971 for Home, a 1972 Southern Baptist Radio and Television Commission film, which dropped his writing credit. Perry built on William Arrowsmith's update of Henry A. Smith's 1887 newspaper reconstruction, published 33 years after a speech Seattle probably gave in 1854. The popular "does not belong to us; we belong to the earth" form is a later modernized version of Perry's text.

quote: The prize is not the trophy, it is who you become as you earned it.
notes: The exact sentence isn't in any Rohn book or dated source. It condenses a lesson Rohn credited to his mentor Earl Shoaff, whom he met in 1955: "Set a goal of becoming a millionaire for what it will make of you to achieve it."

quote: Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.
notes: The actual air-to-ground transmission (past tense); commander Jim Lovell then repeated it. The present tense was in use by 1974 (an ABC TV movie title) and was fixed in memory by the 1995 film Apollo 13, whose writers changed the tense for drama.

quote: Be the change you wish to see in the world.
notes: Not found in Gandhi's writings. The earliest close match is Arleen Lorrance's 1974 "Love Project" ("be the change you want to see happen"), and the earliest Gandhi credit Quote Investigator found is 1987. Gandhi's related idea, translated from a 1913 Gujarati Indian Opinion column: "We but mirror the world... If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change."

quote: Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
notes: The novel's opening line (book form 1878), quoted in Constance Garnett's 1901 translation. In Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997) Jared Diamond turned it into the "Anna Karenina principle": a species must pass every test to be domesticated, which is why so few large mammals were.

quote: The mark of a man was to be able to say at the end, 'I've done my share.'
attribution: Alfred E. Perlman (as reported by David P. Morgan, Trains, July 1983)
notes: David P. Morgan ended his July 1983 Trains memorial to Perlman by writing that Perlman "once observed in 1940" this; a secondhand print report, with no other source found.

quote: All your base are belong to us.
notes: From a non-professional in-house English translation of the intro Toaplan added to the 1991 Mega Drive port of its 1989 arcade shooter, released in English only in Europe. It spread as a forum GIF around 1999 and a February 2001 Newgrounds Flash video; The Register called it "a Net-based cult" that month.

quote: It is not the strongest of the species that survives, nor the most intelligent, but the one most responsive to change.
attribution: Leon C. Megginson, 1963 (often misattributed to Charles Darwin)
notes: No edition of Darwin's Origin of Species contains this line (confirmed via the Darwin Correspondence Project, Quote Investigator, and Wikiquote). Megginson's original wording, from his 1963 presidential address to the Southwestern Social Science Association, was explicitly framed as "according to Darwin" and was further compressed over decades into this now-famous version.

quote: It is said an Eastern monarch once charged his wise men to invent him a sentence, to be ever in view, and which should be true and appropriate in all times and situations. They presented him the words: "And this, too, shall pass away."
notes: From the closing paragraph of Lincoln's address to the Wisconsin State Agricultural Society, Milwaukee, September 30, 1859, introduced with "It is said"; he then adds "let us hope it is not quite true." The ring story was already in English print (Walter Scott's 1813 letter to Byron, an 1838 Southern Churchman item); older Persian and Jewish versions are known through secondary summaries.

quote:
He says the best way out is always through.
And I agree to that, or in so far
As that I can see no way out but through—
Leastways for me—and then they'll be convinced.
attribution: Robert Frost, "A Servant to Servants," North of Boston (1914)
notes: The line is spoken by the exhausted farm-wife narrator's husband Len, not asserted as the poem's own moral — she only half-agrees, fearing her own breakdown. The underlying adage predates Frost: Quote Investigator traces "the only way out is through" to an 1870 Harper's Weekly editorial by George William Curtis.
